name: Hanging / stretching for height
lead: Hanging and stretching for height is a practice in height-focused looksmaxxing communities in which people hang from a pull-up bar, lie or hang on traction and inversion equipment, or follow stretching routines with the aim of decompressing the spine. The goal is to look taller: practitioners hope to recover the length the spine loses through the day, to stand and measure at their fullest, or, in the more ambitious versions, to add lasting height. It is also discussed under the names decompression, spinal decompression and gravity traction.

The idea starts from a well-documented observation. Stature is not constant across a day: in a 1985 study of eight young adults the mean daily variation was about 19 mm (1.1 percent of stature), with more than half of the loss occurring in the first hour after rising and roughly 70 percent regained in the first half of the night.[7] Spine models attribute most of this change to deformation of the intervertebral discs under load.[8] Proponents reason that deliberately unloading the spine, with a hang, an inversion table or a stretch routine, can restore that length sooner or hold more of it.[1][4]

Research on the topic comes mostly from physical therapy rather than from height science. Radiographic studies of inversion in the 1980s measured temporary increases in the spacing between lumbar vertebrae,[9][10] a Cochrane review of mechanical traction for low back pain found little or no effect on pain or function,[12] and reviews of inversion tables describe both a pleasant stretching sensation and a record of reported injuries.[4][13] No published trial has tested hanging or stretching routines as a way to increase adult height. Adult height is described as highly heritable, and long-bone growth stops when the growth plates close in the mid to late teens.[1][15]

chain: Hanging, traction or stretching unloads the spine
Discs take up fluid and vertebral spacing widens
Standing height measures and looks a little taller, mostly for a short time
angle.text: Practitioners hang from a bar, use an inversion table or follow stretch routines to decompress the discs, feel longer through the back and stand at their fullest measured height. Imaging studies show a temporary widening of the spaces between vertebrae, while forum users describe layered routines that they say produce longer-term gains.

paras: Practitioners describe several related activities. The simplest is the dead hang, in which a person hangs from a pull-up bar by the hands with the body relaxed; the pull-up article on Wikipedia describes the dead hang as the bottom position of the pull-up and a progression point toward it.[17] Traction tables and straps apply a pulling force to the spine, inversion tables and gravity boots suspend the body by the ankles at an angle up to fully upside down, and stretching routines use floor or wall positions meant to lengthen the back.[4][18]

Wikipedia defines inversion therapy as hanging by the legs, ankles or feet at an inverted angle and classes it as a form of spinal traction; it describes the body weight as producing a distractive force that slightly and temporarily increases spacing between vertebrae.[4] Traction more broadly is an orthopedic technique that Wikipedia traces to a Greek traction device illustrated in a Byzantine edition of Galen's work, and it is delivered in physical therapy as intermittent or continuous mechanical traction for neck and lower-back problems.[18]

Non-surgical spinal decompression is the term clinics use for physical-therapy traction aimed at disc-related back pain, and Wikipedia lists it alongside surgical options such as microdiscectomy and laminectomy.[3]

sections.h: Mechanism and the daily height cycle
paras: The spine's intervertebral discs have a gel-like core that holds water through glycosaminoglycans and aggrecan, and Wikipedia notes that the amount of these water-binding molecules falls with age and degeneration, a change it links partly to the loss of height in older adults.[14] Wikipedia on human height likewise attributes height loss in older age mainly to disc desiccation, soft-tissue atrophy and postural change, and cites a study of 100 children who were on average about 1.5 cm shorter in the late afternoon than on waking.[1]

Laboratory work gives more detail. In a 1985 study in Spine, Tyrrell, Reilly and Troup measured the stature of eight young adults to the nearest millimetre and found a mean daily variation of 19.3 mm. About 54 percent of the loss happened in the first hour after rising, roughly 70 percent was regained in the first half of the night, shrinkage increased with static shoulder loads of 2.5 to 40 kg, repetitive lifting produced more shrinkage than equal static loading, and recovery lying in a semi-reclined (Fowler's) position was faster than recovery standing.[7]

A 1999 viscoelastic spine model by Keller and Nathan predicted an immediate height loss of 11.7 mm and a total of 19.6 mm (1.1 percent of body height) after eight hours of loading. In the model about two-thirds of the loss occurred immediately and most of it came from disc deformation, with thoracic discs contributing 57 percent and lumbar discs 32 percent.[8] Proponents of decompression read these numbers as showing that a measurable amount of height is recoverable, and some measure themselves at the same time each morning for that reason.[1]

In height-focused communities, hanging is typically described as one part of a routine rather than a stand-alone method. Posts group bar hangs with stretching, posture work, sleep, nutrition and sometimes impact exercise. One guide on looksmax.org presents decompression together with jump-rope sessions and blood-flow restriction in a protocol its author says can add several inches, and says it was refined over two years of experimenting.[5] Another thread on the same forum discusses decompression alongside microfracturing, natural growth and drugs in the context of open growth plates.[6]

A more modest use is cosmetic and day-to-day. A person who hangs for a few minutes before being measured, or who stretches the back after long periods of sitting, may stand a little taller at that moment, and extending the thoracic spine can change how upright someone looks. Practitioners also describe hanging as a way to build grip and shoulder strength, which the pull-up literature treats as a separate benefit; Wikipedia notes that overhead hanging movements reduce the subacromial space and carry a shoulder impingement risk in some variants.[17]

Inversion tables and gravity boots are sold for back comfort and recreational fitness. Wikipedia cites a 1983 Time magazine article, "Hang Ten", on gravity-boot workouts as an early mainstream mention.[4]

In a 1985 study in the Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy, Kane, Karl and Swain inverted 15 healthy men fully for 10 minutes and took lateral X-rays before and after. Separation increased at all measured levels, with statistically significant anterior separation at every level except L3-L4 and significant posterior separation at every level except L1-L2 and L5-S1.[9]

A 1985 crossover study in Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation by Gianakopoulos and colleagues had 20 people with chronic low back pain try three traction devices, two inversion and one upright suspension, for up to 20 minutes each. Inversion distracted the lower lumbar spaces by 0.3 to 4.0 mm, raised systolic blood pressure by an average of 17.2 mmHg and lowered heart rate by about 16 beats per minute, and symptoms improved in 13 of 16 symptomatic patients; the authors recommended medical supervision.[10]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, summarises the radiographic literature as showing short-term gains of roughly 5 to 9 mm after sessions of 20 to 42 minutes that largely reverse within about an hour.[2]

subs.h: Traction and inversion for back pain
paras: The Cochrane review by Wegner and colleagues (2013) included 32 randomized trials with 2,762 participants and concluded that traction, alone or combined with other treatments, had little or no effect on pain, function, global improvement or return to work in low back pain with or without sciatica. Adverse effects were reported in 7 of the 32 studies and included increased pain, worsened neurological signs and later surgery.[12]

A 2012 pilot randomized trial by Prasad and colleagues in Disability and Rehabilitation enrolled people awaiting surgery for single-level lumbar disc disease: 13 were assigned to inversion plus physiotherapy and 11 to physiotherapy alone. At six weeks, 10 of 13 in the inversion group had avoided surgery compared with 2 of 11 controls, with no significant differences in disability, pain, quality of life or MRI findings; the authors called for a larger multicentre trial.[11]

Wikipedia's article on inversion therapy cites a 2021 source saying most people do not get benefit in speed or quality of recovery and that the main benefit is that it feels pleasant, and notes that its principles come from textbooks on traction rather than from inversion-specific trials.[4] Wikipedia also cites a 2022 meta-analysis that found mechanical traction superior to conventional physical therapy in the short term for lumbar disc problems, with inconsistent results after six months.[3][18]

Wikipedia's article on the epiphyseal (growth) plate describes it as the zone where long bones lengthen in children and adolescents, replaced by a bony line when it closes; fusion can occur as early as 12 in girls and 14 in boys, with most girls closing at 14 to 15 and most boys at 15 to 17.[15] Wikipedia on human height reports that adult height is highly heritable (60 to 80 percent in twin studies), that average growth reaches zero around 15 to 16 in females and 18 to 19 in males, and that limited research suggests minor growth in males after 19.[1]

Believers who attempt to add height after puberty argue that spinal length is separate from long-bone growth because the spine's length includes the discs, which can take up or lose fluid. No published trial has tested whether a hanging or stretching routine alters permanent adult stature, and the measured effects in the studies above are described as temporary.[2][9]

Wikipedia notes that inversion raises heart rate, cardiac output, peripheral resistance and venous return, citing a 1992 cardiovascular study, and lists heart disease, high blood pressure, eye disease such as glaucoma and pregnancy as higher-risk conditions. It gives 10 minutes as a recommended maximum, says beginners may need help getting off the apparatus, and describes ankle discomfort after a few minutes and worsened acid reflux.[4] The 1985 inversion study recorded petechiae in one patient, headaches in three, blurred vision in three and contact-lens discomfort in one.[10]

A 2023 review in Disability and Rehabilitation by Kassay, Soliman and Jhawar notes that US Food and Drug Administration reports link inversion tables to serious injuries including spinal cord injury, fractures, lacerations and deaths, and that because manufacturers typically make no medical claims the devices have largely been exempt from FDA regulation.[13]

Hanging motionless from a harness is a separate hazard. Wikipedia describes suspension trauma as fainting that can follow holding a person upright and still in a harness, with symptoms usually after at least 20 minutes of free hanging.[16] A plain bar hang with the hands is a different activity with a different load path, and these sources do not address it directly.

No studies found. No published trial has tested bar hanging or stretching routines as a means of increasing adult height. Related research on inversion, mechanical traction and daily stature variation is summarised under Research.[7][9][12]

lore.intro: Hanging and decompression are discussed in height threads on looksmax.org as free, accessible methods that are often stacked with other techniques; claims range from recovering daily height loss to adding inches.[5][6]

claims.claim: Hanging and decompression can add inches by creating space in the spine
claims.believers: Posters describe hanging, stretching and impact exercises as a combined method aimed at stretching fascia and leaving room for new growth, and one author says he refined it over two years.[5]
claims.experts: Imaging studies report temporary lumbar separation of a few millimetres, and Grokipedia summarises gains of roughly 5 to 9 mm that largely reverse within about an hour; no published trial has tested lasting adult height gain.[2][9]

claims.claim: Decompression restores the height lost during the day
claims.believers: Proponents point to the familiar morning-to-evening difference in height as evidence that the spine compresses and can be re-lengthened.[1]
claims.experts: Daily variation of about 19 mm in adults and 1.5 cm in children is documented, and recovery is fastest lying down; traction studies show short-lived elongation.[1][7][9]

claims.claim: Decompression can be combined with other methods while growth plates are open
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread discusses decompression alongside microfracturing, natural growth and drugs in connection with open growth plates.[6]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that most males' growth plates close at 15 to 17 and average male growth reaches zero around 18 to 19, with limited research suggesting minor growth after 19.[1][15]

claims.claim: An inversion table is a way to relieve back pain and keep the spine healthy
claims.believers: Inversion-table sellers and users describe a stretching sensation and relief; Wikipedia notes the main reported benefit is that it feels pleasant while it is happening.[4]
claims.experts: A pilot trial found fewer surgeries in an inversion group without differences in pain or disability, a Cochrane review found little or no effect of traction on low back pain, and a 2023 review describes FDA-reported injuries.[11][12][13]

claims.claim: Measuring height at a consistent time of day gives a fair picture of stature
claims.believers: Height-forum members commonly measure first thing in the morning, treating that as the fullest reading.[1]
claims.experts: A 1985 study found 54 percent of daily shrinkage occurred in the first hour after rising, supporting the idea that time of day affects measurement.[7]

claims.claim: Hanging by the hands is a low-risk activity
claims.believers: Posters describe bar hangs as free and gentle compared with surgery or drugs.[5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes overhead hanging movements can narrow the subacromial space and lists shoulder impingement as a risk in some pull-up variants, while inversion devices carry cardiovascular and eye cautions.[4][17]

card.summary: Hanging and stretching to decompress the spine for height; any gain reported is brief, and no trial tests lasting growth in adults.
card.note: Reference sources describe only short-term spinal elongation; adult height is largely genetic.

quick.overview:
Hanging or stretching for height means using bar hangs, traction or stretch routines to decompress the spine in the hope of gaining height. It circulates in height-focused looksmaxxing spaces.
Reference sources describe daily height variation of around 1 to 1.5 cm and short-lived elongation after traction, but report no strong evidence of lasting gains in healthy adults.
quick.mechanism: The idea is that gravity compresses the discs through the day and sustained traction restores or lengthens the spine. Measured effects in related research are short-term and largely reverse within about an hour.
quick.risks: Related inversion devices carry documented cautions for people with heart disease, hypertension, glaucoma or pregnancy.
